events.name: FINNBORG
events.explanation: Position jumped 124.6 km in 65 s (implied 3726 kn) while reporting 10.5 kn; limit 40 kn. Physically implausible: possible spoofing, GPS fault, or two transmitters sharing one MMSI.
events.case_study: FINNBORG (154 m cargo, Dutch MMSI) was steaming south down the St. Clair River at a steady 9.1 kn, heading 200°. One report in the middle of that run places the same MMSI 124.6 km away in western Lake Erie, at a different but self-consistent 10.5 kn heading 302°. The very next report is back on the river track. Read in time order, the same MMSI produced three more such stray reports (2023-05-10 twice, 2023-10-20), each in western Lake Erie or the lower Detroit River with plausible transit speeds and headings that progress *up* the shipping route. Meanwhile the real FINNBORG was moored or in the St. Clair River. Most likely explanation: a second transmitter using the same MMSI (a misconfigured unit), or messages from another vessel mis-attributed to it, rather than random GPS noise. The Kalman/IMM tracker rejects these fixes as outliers, so the smoothed track is unaffected.

events.name: SAM LAUD
events.explanation: MMSI 366938760 and MMSI 368161390 stayed within 500 m of each other for 4.2 h, both below 2 kn, away from known ports/anchorages and their usual moorings.
events.case_study: The 193 m laker SAM LAUD sat almost motionless (0.2 kn average) for about 4 hours in the Detroit River near Grosse Ile on 2023-09-28, with the harbour tugs WISCONSIN and PENNSYLVANIA within 500 m throughout. It then departed upbound at 8.6 kn. Kinematically this is a "ship-to-ship meeting away from known ports". In practice it is almost certainly routine tug assistance (docking at a facility the port-zone model did not learn, or help in a tight channel). A useful negative example: rendezvous rules need context about tugs and berths, and the explanation text gives the analyst what they need to dismiss it in seconds.

events.case_study: LINDA JANE II, a commercial fishing vessel, spent 87 minutes in water that at most two training voyages had ever crossed. It produced several similar flags in early October. This is what fishing boats do: they work grounds away from the shipping lanes. The route-deviation detector learns "normal" from all traffic, which is dominated by lakers and ferries in the channels. A per-vessel-type traffic model, or excluding fishing vessels from this rule, would remove such flags. Listed here to show both how the rule explains itself and where it is naive.

events.name: YULIA
events.explanation: Silent for 172 min while moving (10.6 kn before, 9.2 kn after), 13.9 km inside the coverage area; it covered 50.9 km (9.6 kn average) during the silence. Normally 89% of expected reports are received here.
events.case_study: YULIA (184 m cargo, Liberian MMSI) stopped reporting for 172 minutes while crossing Lake St. Clair on 2023-10-14, inside the locked test month. It reappeared 50.9 km further on, consistent with uninterrupted transit at about 9.6 kn. This was not a coverage hole: during the silence, 9 other vessels sent 734 reports from the same area, and the cell normally receives 89% of expected reports. The silence was specific to this vessel. Plausible benign causes include a transponder fault, a power or antenna problem, or the unit being switched off in error. In an operational setting this is exactly the kind of "dark transit" an analyst would want to verify through another source.
